title: A dead mouse
hookLine: a young man turns a dead mouse into a fortune by steady small trades (Jataka 4)

cards: A dead mouse is lying in the street. A wealthy treasurer, on his way to the king, glances down and says out loud: a sharp young man could pick that up and start a business. A passerby might laugh.
One young man, poor and standing close enough to hear, doesn't laugh. He picks the mouse up. That's the fourth tale of the Jataka, and the treasurer is the bodhisatta.

teach.b: First, the mouse. The young man sells it at a tavern, as food for the cat, for one tiny copper coin. That's the whole starting capital.

Second, the trades. With the coin he buys a bit of molasses and a jar of water. He waits for the flower gatherers coming home hot and tired, gives them a drink and a taste of sweetness, and they give him flowers.
He sells the flowers, and does it again. After a storm, he gathers fallen branches from the king's garden and sells the wood to a potter.
He gives water to the grass cutters, and later, when horse dealers come to town, the grass cutters sell him their grass. Each step is tiny; none is clever on its own. Third, the patience.
Bit by bit, watching what people need and waiting for the moment, the young man becomes rich.

teach.h: EACH SMALL TRADE PAYS THE NEXT.
teach.b: Not by luck: by a long line of small, honest trades, each paying for the next. Fourth, the return.

teach.h: BACK TO THE MAN WHO SAID IT.
teach.b: He goes back to the treasurer whose remark started it all, brings him a gift and tells him the story.
The treasurer, delighted, gives him his daughter in marriage, and in time the young man takes his place as treasurer.

The Jataka tells it for a monk who'd been slow and discouraged at the start, and its point is spiritual as much as financial: steady small effort, started with whatever is lying in front of you, adds up.

how: Buddhist teachers tell the tale of the little treasurer as an encouragement to begin practice with whatever is at hand and keep at it steadily.

o: what you begin with, however small
the first prize won in a contest
money borrowed from a rich relative

games.q: you're young and poor. a rich man walking past says a sharp person could start a business with the dead mouse in the street. what do you do?
o: pick it up and find someone who needs it.
ask the rich man for a loan instead.
games.why: he picks it up, sells it for a cat, and turns the coin into water, flowers, wood and grass, until he's rich.

practice: Pick something you've wanted to begin and haven't, because you don't have enough yet: time, money, skill. Look for the dead mouse, the smallest plain piece already in front of you, like five minutes or one page.
Name that one piece, let it be enough for today, and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Starting capital. The dead mouse a poor young man sold for one coin, the whole starting capital that steady small trades turned into a whole new life. Today's word.
